rationale.passage_relevance: Genesis 6:4 says the Nephilim were on the earth in those days and also afterward, then associates the period with mighty men of old, men of renown. The syntax does not unambiguously state that the Nephilim are identical with the offspring or with the mighty men. This evidence supports passage-specific synthesis of Genesis 6:4 while preserving the stated interpretive limits.
rationale.scholarly_interpretation: Numbers 13:33 later uses “Nephilim” in the spies' report, and ancient giant traditions developed in reception. Those later comparisons do not supply a physical description for Genesis 6:4, and the spies' claim is itself a later narrative report. No demonic genealogy or measurements are inferred.
rationale.primary_observation: The verse names Nephilim and separately describes mighty men and men of renown; it supplies no height, anatomy, or physical dimensions.

items.title: Second Temple Watchers reception of Genesis 6
items.claim_text: Second Temple texts such as 1 Enoch 6–16 and Jubilees 5:1–11 develop an angelic/Watchers reading of the “sons of God” episode and its offspring. These texts attest later interpretation rather than adding details to Genesis 6:1–4.

rationale.passage_relevance: Second Temple texts such as 1 Enoch 6–16 and Jubilees 5:1–11 develop an angelic/Watchers reading of the “sons of God” episode and its offspring. These texts attest later interpretation rather than adding details to Genesis 6:1–4. This evidence supports passage-specific synthesis of Genesis 6:1-4 while preserving the stated interpretive limits.
rationale.scholarly_interpretation: The reception history helps explain the long influence of a heavenly-being reading. It must remain diachronically distinct from the immediate wording of Genesis; claims about demons or a fixed angelic cosmology are not presented as facts stated in Genesis.
rationale.primary_observation: Genesis 6:1–4 does not mention Watchers, fallen angels, demonic spirits, or an angelic system; the later texts develop those motifs explicitly.

rationale.passage_relevance: Genesis 6:1–4 calls the male figures *bene ha'elohim* (“sons of God”), distinguishes them from the daughters of humanity, and reports that they take wives. The identity of the figures and the force of the episode remain disputed. This evidence supports passage-specific synthesis of Genesis 6:1-4 while preserving the stated interpretive limits.
rationale.scholarly_interpretation: A divine/heavenly-being reading draws support from comparable biblical uses of “sons of God” for heavenly beings (for example, Job 1:6; 2:1; 38:7) and from ancient divine-council settings. Other historically documented readings identify the figures with Seth's line, royal or tyrannical rulers, or judges/mighty human beings; interpreters differ over how the phrase and the episode relate. These are recorded positions, not interchangeable textual facts. Later Second Temple angel traditions are treated in a separate item. The Job references are comparative context only and are intentionally absent from scripture_references.
rationale.primary_observation: The Hebrew phrase is explicit, while Genesis 6:1–4 itself does not name the figures as Sethites, kings, angels, or demons.
